query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoparticles with a higher degree of local chemical short-range order (LCO) will exhibit enhanced structural and chemical stability under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric service regimes because the LCO creates local energy barriers that slow atomic diffusion and phase segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi‐element, near‐equiatomic single‐phase solid‐solution nanoparticles synthesized via conventional methods (without tailored LCO).
generation.intervention: Introduce controlled thermal treatment or dopant additions during or after synthesis to promote and increase the extent of local chemical ordering in the nanoparticles.
generation.conditions: Service conditions corresponding to catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric applications at 473–1923 K, under inert or controlled atmospheres to minimize extrinsic oxidation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical short‐range order, manifesting as hard atomic motifs and bond energy fluctuations that hinder atomic mobility.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced LCO creates localized energy barriers which pin atoms and dislocations, reducing the diffusivity necessary for phase segregation. This impedes thermally activated coarsening and elemental partitioning, thereby stabilizing the single-phase solid-solution structure even under service temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles engineered to have higher LCO will show a lower rate of phase segregation and chemical inhomogeneity. In performance tests, they will retain their catalytic or thermoelectric activity and single-phase structure significantly better than baseline nanoparticles with less pronounced LCO.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced without specific interventions to enhance local chemical ordering, which are expected to undergo measurable phase segregation and chemical instability under long-term high-temperature operation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism may be overshadowed if extrinsic factors (e.g., high oxygen partial pressures, impurities, or mechanical stresses) dominate the degradation process, or if diffusion pathways exist that are insensitive to LCO-induced barriers.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative degree of LCO necessary for substantial stability enhancement and its universality across different multi-element compositions and service environments are not yet well defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two series of multi-element, near-equiatomic nanoparticles: one group with enhanced LCO via controlled post-synthesis thermal treatments (or dopant schemes) and a control group synthesized under standard conditions with minimal LCO. Expose both groups to service conditions (e.g., 800–1100 K under an inert atmosphere) for an extended period. Characterize the phase composition and microstructure before and after exposure using high-resolution TEM, XRD, and atom probe tomography to assess phase segregation and chemical homogeneity.
measurements: Quantification of local chemical ordering (using, e.g., atom probe tomography or X-ray absorption spectroscopy).
Determination of phase purity and presence of any secondary phases (via XRD and TEM imaging).
Measurement of elemental diffusion or segregation profiles across nanoparticles.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with enhanced LCO do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in phase stability, reduced atomic segregation, or maintain superior catalytic/thermoelectric properties compared to the control group under identical service conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Effect of local chemical order on the irradiation-induced defect evolution in CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy

Abstract: SignificanceHigh-entropy alloys have emerged as promising structural materials for nuclear applications. Among the structural features of high-entropy alloys that may influence their irradiation response, a variable that has not received careful study so far is the internal local chemical order. By combining ion irradiation experiments and atomistic simulation of CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy, here we demonstrate that increased local chemical order (e.g., via thermal aging) significantly enhances their resistance to irradiation damage by narrowing the mobility ratio of irradiation-induced interstitials and vacancies that can facilitate their recombination. This finding opens an avenue to tailor radiation resistance, especially effective as the local chemical order are well suited to affect the evolution of point defects. Strengthening in multi-principal element alloys with local-chemical-order roughened dislocation pathways

Abstract: High-entropy and medium-entropy alloys are presumed to have a configurational entropy as high as that of an ideally mixed solid solution (SS) of multiple elements in near-equal proportions. However, enthalpic interactions inevitably render such chemically disordered SSs rare and metastable, except at very high temperatures. Here we highlight the wide variety of local chemical ordering (LCO) that sets these concentrated SSs apart from traditional solvent-solute ones. Using atomistic simulations, we reveal that the LCO of the multi-principal-element NiCoCr SS changes with alloy processing conditions, producing a wide range of generalized planar fault energies. We show that the LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities. This influences the selection of dislocation pathways in slip, faulting, and twinning, and increases the lattice friction to dislocation motion via a nanoscale segment detrapping mechanism.
